title: NVIDIA Nemotron-TwoTower: A Diffusion-Based Language Model
hook: NVIDIA's open Nemotron-TwoTower bolts a diffusion 'denoiser' tower onto a frozen autoregressive model to fill token blocks in parallel — reportedly 2.42x faster at ~98.7% of baseline quality.
key_points: NVIDIA released Nemotron-TwoTower-30B-A3B, a diffusion-based language model built on the Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B backbone.
Two towers: a frozen autoregressive context tower plus a diffusion denoiser tower that iteratively fills blocks of tokens in parallel.
NVIDIA reports it retains ~98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's aggregate benchmark quality.
It reaches about 2.42x the wall-clock generation throughput of that baseline.
Another sign that block-parallel diffusion decoding is moving toward practical LLM serving.
content_html: NVIDIA released Nemotron-TwoTower-30B-A3B, an unusual diffusion-based language model built on its Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B backbone — and it's a clean illustration of how to bolt parallel generation onto an existing autoregressive model.
extra_html:
The two-tower idea

Instead of generating strictly one token at a time, Nemotron-TwoTower splits the work. A frozen autoregressive context tower provides the conditioning, while a diffusion denoiser tower iteratively fills in blocks of tokens in parallel. Because the denoiser reuses the existing autoregressive model rather than retraining a diffusion LM from scratch, it's a relatively cheap way to add block-parallel decoding to a known-good base.

Why it matters

NVIDIA reports the default mask-diffusion configuration keeps about 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's aggregate benchmark quality while reaching roughly 2.42x its wall-clock generation throughput. Alongside research models trained as diffusion LMs from scratch, this is another signal that block-parallel diffusion decoding is moving from curiosity toward practical, faster LLM serving. Details are in NVIDIA's release, linked via the source.
